newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonian markets calm amid political turbulence.
newsitem.headline: Estonian markets calm amid political turbulence.

text.p: Estonia's financial markets were calm on Friday as the country's coalition government fell apart and the search began for a new one.
Dealers said share prices were up amid little fear that a change of government would mean a change of economic course for the small Baltic state.
Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi was holding talks to form a new government after his partners the Reform Party on Thursday quit the coalition with Vaehi's Coalition Party.
"In general, there has been no reaction," said Tonu Pekk, chief equities dealer at leading bank Hansapank.
"The main thing is that even with a new party, the leading party will still be the Coalition Party," Pekk added.

The Reform Party quit the coalition after Vaehi signed a cooperation pact with leading opposition party, the Centre Party. Commentators say that Vaehi is now likely to try and form a new government with the Centrists.
But the Reform Party says the Centre Party, seen as left-of-centre, may slow reforms. This has been dismissed by Vaehi's spokespeople.
Estonia, the smallest of the Baltic states, is regarded as one of the most committed to economic reform and one of the most successful of the ex-Communist bloc states.

Its gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.3 in the first half of 1996, and inflation has gradually fallen from more than 1,000 percent after the country quit the former Soviet Union to reach 17.2 percent year-on-year in October.
It has a fully-functioning stock market and its currency, the kroon, is pegged at eight to one against the German mark.
Senior trader Otto Tamme of Savings Bank said the lack of market reaction showed that people were looking on the political problems as changes of personality rather than policy.
Over-night rates on the money market were running between 2.95 percent to 3.25 percent, Tamme added.
"I do not think this new government will change anything," said Toomas Tsopp, equities trader at Tallinna Pank.
"I can't see the influence of politics here," he added.
Leading political scientist Rein Toomla said "I am sure some people will say that now our development will stop, but I am not sure about this," Toomla told Reuters.
